activities.anchor: Nothing was "hacked" in the movie sense.
activities.caption: bet before you read on — what actually happened
activities.name: ciaEvilTwinPredict

config.q: The student's bank login crossed the stranger's laptop. In security terms, what happened?
choices: One property of one conversation was violated: the conversation was not private
Her password was cracked by brute force
config.why: No zero-days, no cinematic breach — an evil-twin hotspot removed privacy from one conversation. That is the subject in miniature.

activities.anchor: A bridge never studies its designer's habits and waits for the unguarded afternoon; an attacker does.
activities.caption: nature vs opponent — drag the divider
activities.name: ciaOpponentCompare

config.prompt: What the discipline fights — drag the divider:

before.label: most engineering
before.text: fights nature: gravity, friction, weather — the load just sits there

after.label: cybersecurity
after.text: fights an opponent — intelligent, adaptive, actively trying to defeat you, and patient about timing

config.why: Hence the distinctive answers: layered defences that expect to fail, spending justified by incidents prevented, and vocabulary precise enough for board, auditor and engineer.

activities.caption: pair each enforcement tool with its job
activities.name: ciaConfidentialityMatch

config.prompt: Pair each enforcement tool with its job:

pairs.right: only key holders can read it
everyone agrees what counts as secret
grade records restricted to authorised staff

config.why: Enforcement is everyday — scramble, restrict, classify; the breach is the exception that makes news.

activities.anchor: breaks it just as thoroughly by accident
activities.caption: true or false — what integrity actually means
activities.name: ciaIntegrityJudge

statements.s: Integrity means data truly represents what it is meant to represent — no tampering, no silent corruption, no unauthorised edits.
statements.why: Saying what you mean, consistently — the word is borrowed from personal integrity.

statements.s: Only deliberate attacks break integrity; accidents don't count.
statements.why: A power surge or a slip of the keyboard does it too — property broken is property broken.

statements.s: Cryptographic hashes and digital signatures make any alteration detectable.
statements.why: And audit trails attach a name and a time to every change.

statements.s: Input validation exists to speed up databases.
statements.why: It stops attackers rewriting what a system accepts.

activities.anchor: which is why integrity failures are often the quieter and more dangerous kind
activities.caption: leak or tamper? file each failure
activities.name: ciaBreachSort

config.prompt: Leak or tamper? File each incident:

items.label: a laptop of patient records left in a taxi
a grade changed by a hired hacker

config.why: Leaks expose; tampering steers reality in plain sight.

activities.anchor: repays study because it attacks two properties at once
activities.caption: the routine-looking attachment — walk it
activities.name: ciaRansomBranch

config.root: 9:14 a.m. An attachment arrives that looks like it comes from the top of the company — routine earnings paperwork.

choices.label: It's from the top — open
choices.feedback: The encryption of the company's data begins quietly in the background — the bait worked because it looked routine.

choices.label: Verify through another channel first
choices.feedback: The human is the cheap entry; a thirty-second check closes it.

open.text: Files are locking themselves. Which properties are under attack?

choices.label: Availability (files held hostage) and integrity (restored data may not be trustworthy if attackers spent weeks inside)
choices.feedback: That is why recovery means rebuilding trust, not just restoring files.

choices.label: Only availability — once files are restored, nothing else is wrong
choices.feedback: Restored, yes — but if the attacker spent weeks inside, what you restored may not be trustworthy.

only.text: The second property was there all along — files held hostage, and trust shaken in everything restored.

both.text: Pay-or-restore is the availability decision; proving the network clean is the integrity one.

verify.text: Reported and quarantined. What made this entry so cheap?

choices.label: The human element — phishing works because it looks routine
choices.feedback: Breach surveys find the human element in a large majority of incidents.

choices.label: The firewall must have been off
choices.feedback: The mail filter was on — the message simply looked legitimate; that is the human entry.

human.text: Layered defences expect the first layer to fail — training, filtering, and the verification habit behind them.

firewall.text: Doors are people-shaped more often than port-shaped — verify, report, and let the layers behind you work.

config.why: Availability holds the files hostage; integrity shakes trust in whatever is restored.

activities.anchor: floods of that size are expected roughly once a decade — a rate of 0.1 per year
activities.caption: call the annualised bill
activities.name: ciaFloodEst

config.prompt: A flood doing 200,000 dollars of damage arrives about every ten years — the expected annual bill?
config.why: 200,000 ÷ 10 = 20,000 — a safeguard at 5,000 is justified; at 50,000 it is not.
config.context: Probabilities for rare events are famously uncertain — the arithmetic forces the right questions, not precision.

activities.anchor: which links can we break, and at what cost?
activities.caption: the intrusion as a sequence — break the chain
activities.name: ciaKillChainOrder

config.prompt: One intrusion, start to finish — put the chain in order:
items: The attacker moves sideways toward the data
config.why: Most successful attacks are patient uses of known weaknesses, unpatched systems and reused passwords — not brilliance.
